title: Lease-based work claiming
subtitle: Parallel workers claim work by lease, designed against the dead-tuple behaviour of PostgreSQL's concurrency model, so two workers never process the same item and nothing is lost on a crash.

stats.label: items in flight at once over a two-hour window
ways the conductor slices a job; leased claiming is one
NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs fed by the claimed work

lede: FAFO Core and Function Forge: my probe-generation workload had parallel workers pulling rows of work from PostgreSQL, and two of them collided on the same item. I needed claiming that holds up under tens of millions of items and survives a worker dying mid-batch. I did not want to pay for it with database churn. The obvious pattern, updating a row to claim it and updating it again to release it, leaves dead tuples behind on every cycle, and at that scale the vacuum load becomes its own problem. I added claiming when two workers collided on real work; nothing about it was speculative.
quote: I design concurrency against the real costs of the database underneath, and I put the hard part in a framework so every function inherits it.
evidence: Distributed job orchestration: time-bounded, renewable leases on work items, so a crash neither loses an item nor lets two workers process it, built into the framework once.
PostgreSQL performance tuning: work claiming designed against the dead-tuple cost of claiming and releasing a row by update under heavy concurrency.
High-throughput batch inference: leased claiming that carried tens of millions of work items across 2 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, with 0.7 to 1 M in flight at once.
author: Corey James
